front: State the 2020 ACC/AHA valve staging system for aortic stenosis (Stages A–D).
back: Stage A: at risk (BAV or aortic sclerosis). Stage B: progressive (mild-moderate). Stage C1: asymptomatic severe with preserved LVEF. Stage C2: asymptomatic severe with LVEF < 50%. Stage D1: symptomatic high-gradient severe. Stage D2: symptomatic low-flow/low-gradient severe with reduced EF. Stage D3: symptomatic paradoxical low-flow/low-gradient severe with preserved EF.

front: State the 2020 ACC/AHA Class I indications for AVR in severe aortic stenosis.
back: 1) Symptomatic severe high-gradient AS (D1). 2) Asymptomatic severe AS with LVEF < 50% (C2). 3) Severe AS undergoing other cardiac surgery.

front: What thresholds define 'very severe' aortic stenosis?
back: Peak aortic velocity ≥ 5 m/s (or mean gradient ≥ 60 mmHg). Class IIa indication for AVR even if asymptomatic.

front: Give three imaging findings that trigger consideration of AVR in asymptomatic severe AS despite preserved EF.
back: 1) Abnormal exercise test (BP drop or symptoms). 2) Rapid progression (velocity increase ≥ 0.3 m/s per year). 3) Very severe AS (velocity ≥ 5 m/s). 4) Elevated BNP.

front: Which 2020 ACC/AHA aortic root threshold triggers surgery in BAV patients?
back: Aortic root or ascending aorta > 5.5 cm (any patient). > 5.0 cm if additional risk factors (family history of aortic dissection, growth > 5 mm/year, or coarctation). > 4.5 cm if undergoing AVR for AS/AR.

front: Estimating LV end-diastolic pressure from an AR jet — write the formula.
back: LVEDP = Diastolic BP − 4 × (end-diastolic AR jet velocity)². Normal LVEDP ~ 10–12 mmHg.

front: Describe the CW jet contour of chronic vs acute severe AR.
back: Chronic severe AR: relatively slow deceleration (PHT > 200 ms early on, shortens as chronicity progresses). Acute severe AR: steep deceleration slope (PHT < 200 ms) with rapid diastolic equalization of aortic and LV pressures.

front: Indications for AVR in chronic severe aortic regurgitation?
back: Class I: 1) Symptomatic severe AR. 2) Asymptomatic severe AR with LVEF ≤ 55%. 3) Severe AR undergoing other cardiac surgery. Class IIa: LVESD > 50 mm (or LVESDi > 25 mm/m²).

front: How does isometric handgrip affect an AR murmur?
back: Handgrip increases afterload (SVR) → increases regurgitant gradient → INTENSIFIES the AR murmur. Also intensifies MR. Reduces HCM and MVP murmurs.

front: How does amyl nitrite inhalation affect an AR vs an AS murmur?
back: Amyl nitrite reduces preload and afterload. AR murmur DECREASES (less regurgitant gradient). AS murmur INCREASES (higher gradient across the valve from tachycardia). HCM murmur INCREASES (unmasks obstruction).

front: State the ACC/AHA aortic root replacement thresholds for Marfan syndrome.
back: Aortic root or ascending aorta > 5.0 cm in Marfan. > 4.5 cm if additional risk factors (family history of dissection, growth > 3 mm/year). Loeys-Dietz uses even earlier thresholds.

front: How do you differentiate a suprasternal Doppler descending aortic flow pattern of severe AR from coarctation?
back: Severe AR: holodiastolic reversal in the descending aorta, but normal systolic ejection contour proximally. Coarctation: sustained antegrade DIASTOLIC flow (saw-tooth pattern) distal to the narrowing with elevated peak systolic velocity, and diastolic run-off is preserved (not reversed).

front: Which finding differentiates severe from moderate AR by CW deceleration slope?
back: Pressure half-time (PHT). PHT < 200 ms → severe AR. PHT > 500 ms → mild AR. Reflects rate of LV/aortic diastolic pressure equalization.

front: When is the aortic root measured for growth surveillance?
back: At the sinus of Valsalva in end-diastole (leading-edge to leading-edge, PLAX). Serial studies to detect growth > 3 mm/year (Marfan/genetic aortopathy) or > 5 mm/year (BAV).
